title: 04. Caching: Memcached
summary: Memcached is a simple, high-performance, distributed in-memory key-value cache that stores opaque blob values addressed by string keys, distinguished by its multi-threaded single-port architecture (one process serves many…
objectives: What are the key differences between Memcached and Redis?
Why does Memcached use a slab allocator, and what are its trade-offs?
How does consistent hashing work in Memcached, and why is it needed?
Why doesn't Memcached have persistence, and what are the implications?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Memcached is a simple, high-performance, distributed in-memory key-value cache that stores opaque blob values addressed by string keys, distinguished by its multi-threaded single-port architecture (one process serves many worker threads via a shared hash table), its slab allocator (memory is pre-partitioned into fixed-size chunks to eliminate fragmentation), its LRU eviction per slab class, its complete lack of persistence (data is lost on restart by design), and its client-side consistent-hashing model (the server is a dumb KV store; the client decides which server holds which key) — used at massive scale by Facebook, Wikipedia, YouTube, and Twitter for pure caching workloads where raw throughput and simplicity matter more than Redis's rich data structures.

Memcached is the original in-memory cache, created by Brad Fitzpatrick in 2003 for LiveJournal, and its design philosophy is the opposite of Redis's: where Redis piles on features (data structures, persistence, clustering, pub/sub, Lua), Memcached strips them away. A Memcached server understands exactly five commands that matter — `set`, `get`, `delete`, `add` (set-if-not-exists), and `replace` (set-if-exists) — plus a few utilities (`incr`, `decr`, `stats`, `flush_all`). It stores opaque blobs (any bytes up to 1MB by default) addressed by string keys (up to 250 bytes). It has no data types (the value is just bytes), no persistence (data is lost on restart, by design — Memcached is a cache, not a database), no replication (each key lives on exactly one server), no clustering (the cluster is a client-side fiction, enforced by consistent hashing), and no atomic multi-key operations. The philosophy is: do one thing (cache opaque blobs) and do it extremely well, leaving everything else (sharding, replication, persistence, data structure semantics) to the application or the client library. Real-world: Facebook runs one of the largest Memcached fleets in the world (tens of thousands of servers, billions of operations per second) for caching social graph data, photo metadata, and news feed stories; Wikipedia uses Memcached for rendered page HTML and parsed wikitext; YouTube's early architecture used Memcached for video metadata; Twitter's timeline cache was historically Memcached (later migrated to Redis).

The **multi-threaded architecture** is Memcached's first defining choice and its primary throughput advantage over single-threaded Redis. A Memcached process launches N worker threads (typically one per CPU core, configured via `-t`), all sharing a single hash table protected by per-bucket locks. When a connection arrives, the main thread accepts it and hands it off to a worker thread (via libevent's event loop), which processes all commands on that connection. Because the workers share the hash table, a `set` on one thread is visible to a `get` on another thread immediately (with proper locking). The benefit: a Memcached process can use all CPU cores, so its throughput scales with the core count — a 32-core server can handle 1-2 million operations per second, vs ~100k for a single-threaded Redis instance (before Redis 6's I/O threading, which closes some but not all of the gap). The trade-off: the per-bucket locks can contend under high write load, and the shared hash table requires careful memory management (the slab allocator, below). For pure caching workloads (mostly `get` operations on small values), Memcached's multi-threaded throughput is hard to beat, which is why Facebook and Wikipedia chose it over Redis. Real-world: Facebook's `mcrouter` proxy layer sits in front of thousands of Memcached servers and shards traffic by consistent hashing; the per-server throughput is critical because fewer servers means less network overhead.

The **slab allocator** is Memcached's second defining choice and the source of its memory efficiency. A traditional `malloc`/`free` allocator fragments memory badly under a workload with mixed-size values (e.g., 100-byte and 10KB values interleaved), causing the cache to use 2x its logical size and reducing hit rate. Memcached avoids this by pre-partitioning memory into **slab classes**, each holding chunks of a fixed size: slab class 1 holds 80-byte chunks, class 2 holds 104-byte chunks, class 3 holds 128-byte chunks, and so on, doubling in size (with a growth factor configurable via `-f`, default 1.25). When a `set` arrives, Memcached finds the smallest slab class that fits the value and stores it in a chunk of that class. There is no per-value `malloc` — chunks are pre-allocated and reused (a freed chunk goes back to the slab class's free list). The benefit: zero fragmentation (chunks are always the right size, no half-used pages), fast allocation (just pop a chunk from the free list), and predictable memory usage. The trade-off: **internal fragmentation** within a chunk — a 90-byte value stored in a 104-byte chunk wastes 14 bytes (13%). If the workload has values that don't match the slab boundaries well, this can waste 20-30% of memory. The growth factor `-f` controls the granularity: a smaller factor (1.2) means more slab classes (less waste, more overhead per class); a larger factor (1.5) means fewer classes (more waste, less overhead). Real-world: Facebook tunes the slab sizes for their specific workload (mostly small values <1KB); Wikipedia uses the default; most deployments accept the ~10-20% waste as a fair trade for the simplicity and speed.

The **LRU eviction per slab class** is Memcached's third defining choice and a subtle departure from a naive global LRU. When a slab class fills up (no free chunks), Memcached evicts the least-recently-used chunk *in that slab class*, not globally. The reason: a chunk in class 1 (80 bytes) cannot hold a value from class 3 (128 bytes), so evicting a class 1 chunk to make room for a class 3 value doesn't work — they're different memory pools. The consequence is **slab imbalance**: if the workload has a sudden surge of class-3 values but the memory is mostly class-1 chunks, Memcached cannot reassign class-1 chunks to class-3 (it would have to evict class-1 values to free class-1 chunks, but those chunks are still class-1). This is the famous "slab calcification" problem: once a slab class is allocated, it stays that size, even if the workload shifts. The fix in modern Memcached (2.0+) is the **automove** feature: a background thread monitors slab class utilization and slowly reassigns free chunks from underutilized classes to overutilized ones, but this is conservative (slow migration to avoid thrashing). The trade-off: per-slab LRU is simple and fast (no global lock), but it can cause premature evictions in a shifting workload. Real-world: Facebook's mcrouter and Twitter's twemproxy layer above Memcached work around this by pre-sharding so each shard sees a uniform value size distribution; some deployments run separate Memcached instances for different value sizes (e.g., one for small JSON, one for large HTML).

The **client-side consistent hashing** is Memcached's fourth defining choice and the source of its distributed architecture. Memcached servers are **dumb** — they don't know about each other, they don't shard, they don't replicate. The client library (e.g., `libmemcached` for C/C++, `pymemcache` for Python, `spymemcached` for Java) maintains the list of servers and decides which server holds which key. The naive approach (modulo hashing: `server = hash(key) % N`) breaks when the server count changes (adding or removing a server invalidates ~1/N of all keys, causing a thundering herd of misses). The production approach is **consistent hashing** (invented by Karger et al. at MIT): each server is placed at multiple points on a hash ring (typically 160 virtual nodes per server), and a key is assigned to the next server clockwise on the ring. When a server is added or removed, only the keys on that server's portion of the ring are remapped — typically 1/N of keys, vs 100% for modulo hashing. This makes cluster scaling graceful: adding a server doesn't invalidate the whole cache, just the fraction of keys that move to the new server. The trade-off: consistent hashing has slightly less even distribution than modulo (the virtual nodes approximate but don't guarantee uniformity), and the client must handle server failures (a dead server's keys must be redistributed to the next server on the ring, with a brief cache-miss spike). Real-world: Facebook's mcrouter, Twitter's twemproxy, and the `ketama` algorithm (used by `libmemcached` and most clients) all implement consistent hashing; the `ketama` paper from Last.fm is the canonical reference.

The **lack of persistence** is Memcached's fifth defining choice and the source of its operational simplicity. Memcached stores data only in RAM; on restart (planned or crash), all data is lost. This is by design: Memcached is a cache, not a database, and persistence would add complexity (disk I/O, recovery logic, durability trade-offs) for a feature that caches don't need. If a Memcached server crashes, the application's cache miss rate spikes (the dead server's keys are now misses), but the database (the source of truth) serves them and the cache repopulates over a few minutes. To mitigate: (1) Run multiple Memcached servers (consistent hashing means a single server crash only affects 1/N of keys); (2) Have a pre-warming strategy (after a restart, proactively repopulate the hot keys); (3) Use a circuit breaker to protect the database during the cache-miss spike. The contrast with Redis (which offers RDB and AOF persistence) is stark: Redis can serve as a database (with persistence), while Memcached is strictly a cache. The choice between them often comes down to "do I need persistence?" — if yes, Redis; if no, Memcached. Real-world: Facebook's Memcached fleet treats each server as disposable — when one dies, mcrouter reroutes traffic and the cache repopulates from the databases; Wikipedia's Memcached servers are restarted regularly (for OS patches) without user impact because the cache is warm within minutes.

The **typical production use cases** are: (1) **Object caching** — caching database query results, user objects, session data as opaque blobs (the application serializes to JSON/MessagePack before `set`, deserializes after `get`). This is the most common use; Facebook caches social graph objects, Wikipedia caches parsed wikitext. (2) **HTML fragment caching** — caching rendered HTML fragments (a sidebar, a product card) to skip the rendering step on cache hit. Wikipedia caches full page HTML for anonymous users. (3) **Session storage** — Memcached's speed and simplicity make it a popular session store, though the lack of persistence means sessions are lost on restart (acceptable for low-value sessions). (4) **Rate limiting counters** — `incr`/`decr` on a key with a TTL provides a simple fixed-window rate limiter. (5) **Lock coordination** — `add` (set-if-not-exists) with a TTL provides a simple distributed lock (though Redis's richer locking primitives are usually preferred). The trade-offs vs Redis: Memcached is faster for pure get/set (multi-threaded, simpler protocol), uses less memory per key (no data structure overhead), and is operationally simpler (no persistence, no clustering, no scripting); Redis is richer (data structures, persistence, clustering, pub/sub, Lua), more durable (persistence), and more versatile (leaderboards, streams, rate limiters). The choice: use Memcached for pure caching workloads where throughput and simplicity matter most; use Redis for richer use cases (data structures, persistence, pub/sub). Real-world: Facebook, Wikipedia, and early Twitter chose Memcached for its raw throughput; newer companies default to Redis for its versatility.

(10 bytes value + overhead) v Slab Allocator: class 1 has free chunks? -> yes -> pop one, store value class 1 full? -> evict LRU chunk in class 1, reuse it | v Hash table (per-bucket lock): bucket[hash("user:1") % buckets] -> entry -> slab chunk ptr | v Response: STORED\r\n Slab classes (example, growth factor 1.25): class 1: chunk size 80B (for values 1-72B after overhead) class 2: chunk size 104B (for values 73-96B) class 3: chunk size 128B (for values 97-120B) class 4: chunk size 160B (for values 121-152B) ... class 40: chunk size 1MB (for values up to ~1MB) Internal fragmentation: 90B value in class 3 (128B chunk) -> 38B wasted (30%) But: zero external fragmentation (no malloc/free, chunks pre-allocated) Consistent hashing ring (client-side): ring: [0, 2^32) server1 placed at 100, 250, 400, 550, ... (160 virtual nodes) server2 placed at 150, 300, 450, 600, ... server3 placed at 200, 350, 500, 650, ... hash("user:1") = 280 -> next clockwise = server1 (at 400) -> MC1 hash("user:2") = 320 -> next clockwise = server2 (at 450) -> MC2 hash("user:3") = 480 -> next clockwise = server3 (at 500) -> MC3 Add server4 (at 280, 430, 580, ...): "user:1" (hash 280) -> now goes to server4 (at 280), not server1 Only ~1/N keys remap (graceful scaling), not 100% like modulo hashing ``` ### Walkthrough 1. **Client computes the target server**: The application calls `mc.set("user:1", b"")`. The client library computes `hash("user:1") = 280` and looks up the next server clockwise on the consistent hash ring — say, server 1 (at position 400). The client opens a TCP connection to server 1 (or reuses a pooled connection) and sends the `set` command. 2. **Server receives and dispatches to a worker thread**: Server 1's main thread (running libevent) accepts the connection and hands it to an idle worker thread (e.g., worker 3). The worker parses the command (`set user:1 0 3600 10` followed by a 10-byte value). 3. **Slab allocator stores the value, LRU evicts if needed**: The worker finds the smallest slab class that fits the value (class 1, 80-byte chunks, for a 10-byte value). If class 1 has a free chunk, it pops one and stores the value; if class 1 is full, it evicts the LRU chunk in class 1 (per-slab LRU, not global) and reuses it. The hash table is updated to point `user:1` to the slab chunk. The worker sends `STORED\r\n` back to the client.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- A pool of fixed-size chunks with per-slab LRU eviction.
- Multi-threaded KV cache with slab allocator and per-slab LRU.
- Ketama-style consistent hashing: 160 virtual nodes per server.
- Client that uses consistent hashing to pick a server per key.
- A simplified Memcached-like server demonstrating:
- Multi-threaded architecture (worker pool sharing a hash table)
- Slab allocator (pre-allocated chunks per size class)
- Client-side consistent hashing (in a separate client class)

**Defines:** `SlabClass`, `MemcachedServer`, `ConsistentHashRing`, `MemcachedClient`

```python
# A simplified Memcached-like server demonstrating:
# - Multi-threaded architecture (worker pool sharing a hash table)
# - Slab allocator (pre-allocated chunks per size class)
# - Per-slab LRU eviction
# - Client-side consistent hashing (in a separate client class)

import hashlib
import bisect
import threading
import time
from collections import OrderedDict, defaultdict

# ---------- Slab allocator with per-slab LRU ---------- #
class SlabClass:
    """A pool of fixed-size chunks with per-slab LRU eviction."""

    def __init__(self, chunk_size: int, max_chunks: int):
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size
        self.max_chunks = max_chunks
        # key -> value, ordered by insertion (LRU at front).
        self.entries: OrderedDict[str, bytes] = OrderedDict()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.evictions = 0

    def fits(self, value_size: int) -> bool:
        return value_size + 32 <= self.chunk_size  # 32B overhead per entry

    def set(self, key: str, value: bytes) -> bool:
        with self.lock:
            if key in self.entries:
                self.entries.move_to_end(key)  # refresh LRU
                self.entries[key] = value
                return True
            if len(self.entries) >= self.max_chunks:
                self.entries.popitem(last=False)  # evict LRU
                self.evictions += 1
            self.entries[key] = value
            return True

    def get(self, key: str):
        with self.lock:
            if key not in self.entries:
                return None
            self.entries.move_to_end(key)  # refresh LRU
            return self.entries[key]

    def delete(self, key: str) -> bool:
        with self.lock:
            return self.entries.pop(key, None) is not None

class MemcachedServer:
    """Multi-threaded KV cache with slab allocator and per-slab LRU."""

    def __init__(self, mem_limit: int = 64 * 1024 * 1024,  # 64MB
                 growth_factor: float = 1.25, min_chunk: int = 80):
        # Build slab classes: 80B, 100B, 125B, ... up to 1MB.
        self.slab_classes: list[SlabClass] = []
        size = min_chunk
        while size <= 1024 * 1024:
            chunks_per_slab = max(1, mem_limit // size // 10)  # distribute
            self.slab_classes.append(SlabClass(size, chunks_per_slab))
            size = int(size * growth_factor)
        self.hash_table: dict[str, SlabClass] = {}  # key -> owning slab
        self.table_lock = threading.Lock()
        self.stats = defaultdict(int)

    def _find_slab(self, value_size: int) -> SlabClass:
        for slab in self.slab_classes:
            if slab.fits(value_size):
                return slab
        return self.slab_classes[-1]  # largest slab (or reject if > 1MB)

    def set(self, key: str, value: bytes, ttl: int = 0) -> bool:
        self.stats["sets"] += 1
        if len(value) > 1024 * 1024:
            return False  # value too large (>1MB)
        slab = self._find_slab(len(value))
        with self.table_lock:
            old_slab = self.hash_table.get(key)
            if old_slab is not None and old_slab is not slab:
                old_slab.delete(key)  # value changed size, move slabs
            self.hash_table[key] = slab
        return slab.set(key, value)

    def get(self, key: str):
        self.stats["gets"] += 1
        with self.table_lock:
            slab = self.hash_table.get(key)
        if slab is None:
            self.stats["misses"] += 1
            return None
        value = slab.get(key)
        if value is None:
            self.stats["misses"] += 1
            with self.table_lock:
                self.hash_table.pop(key, None)
        else:
            self.stats["hits"] += 1
        return value

    def delete(self, key: str) -> bool:
        self.stats["deletes"] += 1
        with self.table_lock:
            slab = self.hash_table.pop(key, None)
        return slab.delete(key) if slab else False

# ---------- Client-side consistent hashing ---------- #
class ConsistentHashRing:
    """Ketama-style consistent hashing: 160 virtual nodes per server."""

    def __init__(self, servers: list[str], virtual_nodes: int = 160):
        self.ring: dict[int, str] = {}
        self.sorted_keys: list[int] = []
        for server in servers:
            for vn in range(virtual_nodes):
                key = f"{server}:{vn}"
                h = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % (2**32)
                self.ring[h] = server
                bisect.insort(self.sorted_keys, h)

    def get_server(self, key: str) -> str:
        if not self.sorted_keys:
            raise RuntimeError("no servers in ring")
        h = int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % (2**32)
        idx = bisect.bisect(self.sorted_keys, h)
        if idx == len(self.sorted_keys):
            idx = 0
        return self.ring[self.sorted_keys[idx]]

class MemcachedClient:
    """Client that uses consistent hashing to pick a server per key."""

    def __init__(self, servers: dict[str, MemcachedServer]):
        self.servers = servers
        self.ring = ConsistentHashRing(list(servers.keys()))

    def set(self, key: str, value: bytes, ttl: int = 0) -> bool:
        server_name = self.ring.get_server(key)
        return self.servers[server_name].set(key, value, ttl)

    def get(self, key: str):
        server_name = self.ring.get_server(key)
        return self.servers[server_name].get(key)

# ---------- Demo ---------- #
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Three Memcached servers, each with its own slab allocator.
    servers = {
        "mc1": MemcachedServer(mem_limit=16 * 1024 * 1024),
        "mc2": MemcachedServer(mem_limit=16 * 1024 * 1024),
        "mc3": MemcachedServer(mem_limit=16 * 1024 * 1024),
    }
    client = MemcachedClient(servers)

    # Write 1000 keys of varying sizes.
    for i in range(1000):
        key = f"user:{i}"
        value = f"value-{i}-" + "x" * (i % 200)  # sizes 0-200 bytes
        client.set(key, value.encode())

    # Read them back; verify consistent routing.
    hits = sum(1 for i in range(1000) if client.get(f"user:{i}") is not None)
    print(f"Hit rate: {hits}/1000 = {hits/10:.1f}%")

    # Show which server holds each key (consistent hashing).
    for i in [0, 100, 500, 999]:
        key = f"user:{i}"
        server = client.ring.get_server(key)
        print(f"  {key} -> {server}")

    # Show per-server stats (slab eviction behavior).
    for name, srv in servers.items():
        total_evictions = sum(s.evictions for s in srv.slab_classes)
        print(f"  {name}: gets={srv.stats['gets']} hits={srv.stats['hits']} "
              f"misses={srv.stats['misses']} evictions={total_evictions}")
```

The scenario: at startup, Memcached sees a workload of mostly 80-byte values, so it allocates most of its memory to class 1 (80-byte chunks).
